q: Fluid X holds 150 mmol/L of sodium chloride. Fluid Y holds 150 mmol/L of a molecule that stays whole when it dissolves. How do their osmolarities compare?
options: They are equal: 150 mOsm/L each
X is about 300 mOsm/L and Y is about 150 mOsm/L
Y is higher than X
X is about 150 mOsm/L and Y is about 300 mOsm/L
misconception: osmolarity equals the concentration of the solute

q: A patient's blood sodium is 140 mmol/L. A nursing student estimates her blood osmolality as 2 × 140 = 280 mOsm/kg, and the measured value is 288 mOsm/kg. Why does doubling the sodium give such a close estimate?
options: Each sodium ion has a partner anion; together they are most particles
Each sodium ion splits into two separate particles when it dissolves in the blood
Sodium is counted twice because it carries a charge of +2
Osmolality is defined as twice the sodium concentration

q: Mrs. Lindqvist, 88, lives alone and has barely drunk anything for three days. Her blood sodium is high. Which conclusion does that result best support?
options: She must have eaten a large amount of sodium chloride recently
Her body contains far more sodium than normal
Her body water has fallen, concentrating the sodium she has
Her sodium ions have gained extra charge
misconception: a high concentration means the body holds too much of that substance

q: Put these steps in order to show how a crystal of sodium chloride dissolves in the water of an IV bag.
options: Water molecules crowd the surface of the crystal
Partly negative oxygen ends face the Na+ ions and partly positive hydrogen ends face the Cl− ions
Many small attractions pull individual ions out of the crystal
Each freed ion is surrounded by a shell of water molecules
The ions spread evenly through the water, forming a solution

q: This pathway explains how sweat cools your skin. Which step is wrong?
options: Heat flows from your skin into the film of sweat
The heat breaks covalent bonds inside each water molecule
Water molecules freed from their neighbors escape into the air as vapor
The escaping molecules carry that heat away, so your skin cools

q: Fill the gap: 154 mmol of sodium chloride dissolves in 1 liter of water → ______ → the osmolarity is about 308 mOsm/L
options: Each unit of sodium chloride separates into two ions, Na+ and Cl−
Each unit of sodium chloride stays whole as one single particle in water
The water molecules split into two particles each
The sodium ions pair up, halving the particle count

q: A thin film of water lines the tiny air sacs of your lungs. Its surface tension pulls inward on each sac. What produces that surface tension?
options: Ions in the film repel the air in the sac
Hydrogen bonds pull surface molecules inward toward those below
Covalent bonds link the water molecules into a solid sheet
Air pressure packs the water molecules more tightly

q: A cell joins two glucose molecules into one molecule of maltose by dehydration synthesis. Besides maltose, what does the reaction produce?
options: One molecule of water
One hydrogen ion
One molecule of carbon dioxide
One molecule of ATP

q: During digestion, table sugar (sucrose) is split into glucose and fructose before it is absorbed. Which describes that reaction?
options: Dehydration synthesis, which releases one water molecule
Denaturation, which unfolds the sucrose without breaking bonds
Hydrolysis, which uses up one water molecule
Dehydration synthesis, which uses up one water molecule

q: Jordan, 19, is shaky and sweaty during a run because the glucose level in his blood has fallen. Glucose gel steadies him within minutes, faster than a starchy granola bar would. Why does the gel act faster?
options: Starch is a lipid, which cannot be absorbed
Glucose is already a monosaccharide and needs no hydrolysis
Glucose is hydrophobic, so it slips into the blood more easily
Starch must be denatured by heat before it can be absorbed
misconception: all carbohydrates reach the blood equally fast

q: Mr. Hale, 45, eats dinner at 7 p.m. and nothing more until breakfast. Overnight, the glucose level in his blood stays in its normal range. Which store supplies that glucose?
options: Glycogen in his muscles
Cholesterol in the boundary around his cells
Triglycerides split directly into glucose
Glycogen in his liver

q: Glycogen is far more branched than plant starch. How does that branching affect the way a liver cell uses it?
options: It makes glycogen hydrophobic, so it stays out of the cell's water
It lets glycogen hold fat as well as glucose
Many branch ends let glucose be released from many points at once
It makes glycogen impossible to break down

q: Which of these are lipids? Select all that apply.
options: Cholesterol
Glycogen
A triglyceride
An amino acid
A phospholipid

q: Butter is solid at room temperature, but olive oil pours. What difference in their fatty acids explains this?
options: Olive oil's fatty acids carry charges that repel each other
Olive oil's fatty acids have more double bonds, which bend the chains
Butter's fatty acids are linked by peptide bonds
Butter contains glycogen, which hardens it

q: A saturated fatty acid chain is changed so that one pair of its carbons now shares a double bond, bent as in natural fats. Predict the change in each variable.

variables.name: Number of hydrogen atoms on the chain
How tightly many such chains pack together
Number of carbon atoms in the chain

q: Phospholipids dropped into water form a two-layer sheet with their heads on both outer faces and their tails inside. What drives that arrangement?
options: The tails form covalent bonds with each other across the sheet
The heads are nonpolar and are pushed out of the water
The tails carry charges that attract the tails of the other layer
Water bonds with the heads and itself, squeezing tails together

q: Put these steps in order, from a string of amino acids to a working protein made of four chains.
options: Peptide bonds link amino acids in a set sequence
Hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms coil stretches into helices and fold others into pleated sheets
The whole chain folds into a compact shape, with nonpolar side chains clustered inside
Four folded chains fit together into one working unit

q: During a heat wave, Mr. Osei, 80, is found with a body temperature of 42 °C, measured deep in his body. Some of his proteins stop working. What has happened to those proteins?
options: Weak bonds holding their folded shape broke; their sequence is unchanged
Their peptide bonds broke, releasing free amino acids
Their amino acids were converted into glucose
Their side chains became nonpolar
misconception: denaturation breaks a protein into amino acids

q: This pathway explains how cooking an egg white turns it solid and white. Which step is wrong?
options: Heat makes the egg white's protein molecules move faster
Hydrogen bonds holding each protein's folded shape break
Peptide bonds break, and each protein falls apart into free amino acids
The unfolded chains tangle together, and the egg white turns solid and opaque

q: A protein folds in the watery interior of a cell. Where are its amino acids with nonpolar side chains most likely to end up?
options: Spread evenly over the outer surface
Clustered in the interior of the fold
Released from the chain into the water
Bonded to the water molecules around the protein

q: What are the three parts of a nucleotide?
options: An amino group, a carboxyl group and a side chain
Glycerol and two fatty acids
Four fused carbon rings
A phosphate group, a five-carbon sugar and a nitrogenous base

q: A strand of nucleic acid contains the sugar ribose and the base uracil. Which nucleic acid is it?
options: Ribonucleic acid
Deoxyribonucleic acid
A polysaccharide
A polypeptide

q: Your thigh muscle shortens as you climb a stair, using energy from ATP. What happens to the ATP molecule?
options: Its adenine base is removed, leaving a sugar-phosphate chain
It gains a fourth phosphate group
Its outer phosphate is split off by hydrolysis, leaving ADP
It is linked to other ATP molecules to form a nucleic acid

q: Your body stores much more energy as triglycerides than as glycogen. Which feature of triglycerides makes them the more compact long-term store?
options: They dissolve easily in blood, so they are always ready to use
They are polymers of glucose with extra branches
They contain nitrogen, which holds extra energy
About 9 kcal per gram, stored with almost no water

q: Fill the gap: Glucose from a meal enters the blood → it reaches liver cells → ______ → the liver holds a store of glycogen
options: Liver cells hydrolyze glucose into smaller sugars
Liver cells join glucose by dehydration synthesis
Liver cells denature the glucose into a branched shape
Liver cells link glucose units with peptide bonds

q: An unknown molecule from a cell contains carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and some sulfur. It is a chain built from 20 kinds of unit. What kind of molecule is it?
options: A protein
A carbohydrate
A triglyceride
A nucleic acid

q: A protein that works normally in blood is placed in a fluid with a much higher concentration of hydrogen ions, and it stops working. Which bonds inside the protein are most directly disrupted?
options: The peptide bonds between amino acids
The covalent bonds within each side chain
Ionic bonds between charged side chains
The covalent bonds between carbon and hydrogen

q: What makes a substance an acid?
options: It takes up hydrogen ions from the fluid around it
It releases hydrogen ions when it dissolves in water
It separates into ions other than H+ and OH−
It keeps the pH of a fluid from changing

q: A sample of urine has a pH of 5, and a sample of fluid from inside the small bowel has a pH of 7. How does their hydrogen ion concentration compare?
options: The pH 7 fluid has 2 times more hydrogen ions
The pH 5 fluid has 2 times more hydrogen ions
The pH 7 fluid has 100 times more hydrogen ions
The pH 5 fluid has 100 times more hydrogen ions
misconception: the pH scale is linear

q: A solution has a hydrogen ion concentration of 0.00001 mol/L (10⁻⁵ mol/L). What is its pH, and is it acidic or basic?
options: pH 9, basic
pH 5, basic
pH 5, acidic
pH −5, acidic

q: Mr. Brennan, 63, is found in severe shock. His blood pH is 7.10; a normal value is 7.40. What has happened to the hydrogen ion concentration of his blood?
options: It has roughly doubled
It has risen by about 4%
It has roughly halved
It has risen about 30-fold
misconception: the pH scale is linear

q: What is the normal pH range of blood from an artery?
options: 7.00 exactly

q: Ms. Adeyemi, 40, has a blood pH of 7.29. Which term describes the state of her blood?
options: Alkalemia
Normal blood pH
Neutral
Acidemia

q: Mr. Farouk, 35, has vomited stomach fluid (about pH 2) many times over two days. His tingling fingers and muscle cramps suggest a change in his blood pH. Which change is most likely?
options: His blood pH has risen, because he has lost hydrogen ions
His blood pH has fallen, because he has lost a strong acid
His blood pH is unchanged, because stomach fluid never mixes with blood
His blood pH has fallen, because he has gained hydroxide ions

q: Why can a blood pH outside 7.35 to 7.45 disturb so many body functions at once?
options: Hydrogen ions break the peptide bonds of every protein
Extra hydrogen ions dissolve the fats around each cell
Hydrogen ions change side-chain charges, altering the shape of proteins
Acidic blood cannot carry water to the cells

q: Two beakers each hold one liter at pH 7.4: one of pure water adjusted to that pH, and one containing bicarbonate and carbonic acid. You add the same small amount of strong acid to each. Predict the change in each variable.

variables.name: Free hydrogen ions in the unbuffered water
Carbonic acid in the buffered beaker

q: Hydrogen chloride dissolved in water (HCl) is mixed with sodium hydroxide (NaOH) in equal amounts. What are the products?
options: Sodium chloride and water
Hydrogen gas and sodium
Carbonic acid and chloride
A buffer of HCl and NaOH

q: Put these steps in order to show how your blood handles a burst of hydrogen ions from working muscle.
options: Extra hydrogen ions enter the blood
Bicarbonate takes up the hydrogen ions
Carbonic acid forms and holds most of those hydrogen ions
Carbonic acid splits into carbon dioxide and water
The lungs breathe the carbon dioxide out

q: This pathway describes the carbonic acid–bicarbonate buffer handling a strong acid. Which step is wrong?
options: A strong acid releases hydrogen ions into the blood
Bicarbonate releases more hydrogen ions to balance them
Carbonic acid forms and holds on to most of the added hydrogen ions
The pH falls far less than it would in unbuffered water

q: Solution A holds 0.01 mol/L of hydrogen chloride. Solution B holds 0.01 mol/L of carbonic acid. Which has the lower pH?
options: Neither; equal concentrations of acid give equal pH
Solution B, because carbonic acid holds on to its hydrogen ions
Solution A, since hydrogen chloride is a strong acid
Solution B, because carbonic acid contains more atoms per molecule

q: A patient with a long-running illness produces extra acid every day. For a while his blood pH stays near normal, but his blood bicarbonate level falls steadily. Then his pH starts to drop quickly. What best explains this pattern?
options: His buffer was working in reverse and releasing acid
Each buffered H+ used up a bicarbonate; few were left
Bicarbonate turned into a strong acid once its level fell
The pH scale becomes linear below 7.35

q: Fill the gap: A strong base adds hydroxide ions (OH−) to buffered blood → OH− takes up free H+, forming water → ______ → pH rises only slightly
options: Bicarbonate releases hydroxide ions of its own
Carbon dioxide is breathed out faster
Salt forms and absorbs the extra base
Carbonic acid releases H+ to replace them and becomes bicarbonate

q: Which of these act as bases in water, taking up hydrogen ions directly or by releasing hydroxide? Select all that apply.
options: Bicarbonate ion (HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>)
Sodium chloride (NaCl)
Sodium hydroxide (NaOH)
Hydrogen chloride (HCl)
Hydroxide ion (OH−)

q: You add 1 mL of a 1 mol/L strong acid to a liter of pure water, and the same amount to a liter of blood in a living person. Which result do you expect?
options: Both fall to about pH 3
The water falls to about pH 3; the blood falls by only a few hundredths
The blood falls further than the water, because blood already holds acid
Neither changes, because 1 mL is too little to matter

q: Normal blood pH is about 7.4. Compared with pure water at pH 7, what does that mean?
options: Blood has slightly more hydrogen ions and is slightly acidic
Blood and pure water have the same number of hydrogen ions
Blood has about 4 times as many hydrogen ions as pure water
Blood has fewer hydrogen ions and is slightly basic

q: Mrs. Lindgren, 70, has a blood pH of 7.52. Which symptoms would you most expect from this change?
options: Tingling around the mouth and muscle cramps
Drowsiness sliding toward coma
Weaker heart contractions with no other signs
No symptoms, because the value is within the normal range

q: What does an enzyme change about the reaction it catalyzes?
options: The activation energy the reactants need to get over
The total energy released when reactants become products
The balance point the reaction settles at when it reaches equilibrium
Whether the overall reaction releases energy or needs an energy input
misconception: enzymes supply energy to a reaction

q: A 45-year-old man drank windshield washer fluid containing methanol two hours ago. His blood pH is still normal. The team gives fomepizole, a drug that binds the active site of alcohol dehydrogenase, the liver enzyme that oxidizes methanol to formaldehyde. Formaldehyde is then oxidized to formic acid. What is the main effect of the drug?
options: It speeds the conversion of methanol into harmless products
It keeps methanol from being oxidized into formaldehyde and then formic acid
It neutralizes formic acid that has already formed in his blood
It shifts the equilibrium of the enzyme reaction back toward methanol

q: In a test tube, alcohol dehydrogenase is working slowly on a small amount of methanol in the presence of fomepizole, a competitive inhibitor. You add a large excess of methanol. What happens to the reaction rate?
options: It stays low: the inhibitor has permanently changed the enzyme's shape
It falls further: extra substrate crowds the enzyme and blocks the active site
It rises: methanol molecules now outnumber the inhibitor at the active site
It stays low: the enzyme was already working at its maximum rate

q: The figure shows the energy during a reaction without an enzyme (left) and with one (right). Which quantity is the same in both panels?
options: The height of the energy hill the reactants have to climb
The number of reactant molecules that react each second
The difference in energy between the reactants and the products
The time the reaction takes to reach equilibrium

fig.alt: Two energy graphs side by side, each plotting energy against the progress of a reaction. Without an enzyme, the reactants must climb a tall hump before falling to the lower energy of the products. With an enzyme, the hump is much lower, while the starting and ending energies are the same as before.

q: A human enzyme and its substrate are held at 60 °C for 30 minutes, and the reaction is then measured at 60 °C. Predict each value compared with the same enzyme measured at 37 °C.

variables.name: Enzyme molecules with a working active site
Energy released per reaction (products compared with reactants)

misconception: heat always speeds enzyme reactions

q: An enzyme is working in a test tube at 30 °C and at pH 7.4, its optimum pH, with a small amount of substrate. Which changes would raise the reaction rate? Select all that apply.
options: Adding more substrate
Warming the tube to 37 °C
Adding a competitive inhibitor
Adding more of the enzyme
Lowering the pH to 5

q: Put the steps of an enzyme reaction in order.
options: The substrate collides with the enzyme and fits into the active site
The enzyme's shape shifts slightly, closing around the substrate
The active site lowers the activation energy and the reaction occurs
The products are released from the active site
The unchanged enzyme binds a new substrate molecule

q: Fill the gap in this chain. Catabolic reactions break down glucose and release energy → ______ → ATP hydrolysis releases energy → anabolic reactions join amino acids into proteins.
options: ADP and phosphate are joined to form ATP
ATP is split into ADP and phosphate
Glucose molecules are linked into glycogen
Enzymes add their own energy to the reactants

q: This description of how alcohol dehydrogenase handles methanol contains one wrong step. Find it.
options: Methanol binds the active site of alcohol dehydrogenase.
The enzyme removes two hydrogen atoms, with their electrons, from methanol.
Methanol gains those electrons, so it is reduced to formaldehyde.
NAD+ accepts the electrons and becomes NADH.
The enzyme releases formaldehyde and is ready to act again.

q: After a meal, your liver links many glucose molecules into glycogen. How is this reaction classified?
options: Catabolic and exergonic
Anabolic and exergonic
Catabolic and endergonic
Anabolic and endergonic

q: A reversible reaction in a sealed flask has reached chemical equilibrium. Which statement about the flask is true?
options: The forward and reverse reactions have both stopped
The amounts of reactants and products are equal
The forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates
Adding an enzyme would raise the amount of product present
misconception: at equilibrium the reaction has stopped

q: In your blood, CO2 + H2O ⇌ carbonic acid ⇌ bicarbonate + H+. A person breathes much faster and deeper than usual for a minute, which removes carbon dioxide from the blood faster than it is made. Predict each change.
In an experiment with a fixed amount of enzyme, the substrate concentration is already high. Doubling it again does not change the reaction rate. What best explains this?
options: Every active site is already occupied nearly all the time
The extra substrate has started to denature the enzyme
The reaction has become endergonic at high substrate levels
The extra substrate has lowered the pH below the enzyme's optimum

q: A 58-year-old man with years of heavy drinking and a very poor diet has a severe deficiency of niacin, the vitamin used to make NAD+. Which reactions are most directly slowed?
options: Reactions that move a phosphate group from ATP onto glucose
Reactions that depend on hydrogen bonds to hold a protein's shape
Oxidation reactions that hand electrons to an electron carrier
Reactions that split ATP into ADP and phosphate

q: Which of these is a cofactor but not a coenzyme?
options: NAD+
FAD
The enzyme's own substrate
A magnesium ion (Mg2+)

q: Where does the energy released by ATP hydrolysis come from?
options: From breaking the bond that holds the end phosphate onto ATP
From the products (ADP and phosphate) holding less energy than ATP and water did
From the ATPase adding its own energy as it splits ATP
From heat taken up from the surrounding fluid
misconception: ATP holds energy in a high-energy bond that releases energy when broken

q: An enzyme that works in the stomach has an optimum pH of about 2. In a test, it is placed in a solution at pH 7.4. What happens to its activity?
options: It falls: the change in H+ alters charges in and around its active site
It rises: pH 7.4 is the normal pH of blood
It is unchanged: pH affects the substrate but not the enzyme
It falls: the enzyme is used up faster at higher pH

q: Which statements about enzymes are true? Select all that apply.
options: They come out of a reaction unchanged and can be reused
They speed the forward and reverse reactions by the same factor
They supply the energy an endergonic reaction needs
They shift a reaction's equilibrium toward the products
Their activity depends on the shape of their active site
misconception: enzymes shift equilibrium or supply energy

q: When glucose enters a cell, an enzyme catalyzes: ATP + glucose → ADP + glucose phosphate. Which description fits this reaction?
options: A decomposition reaction that releases free phosphate into the surrounding water
A synthesis reaction that builds glycogen
An oxidation of glucose in which ATP accepts electrons
An exchange reaction in which a phosphate group moves between molecules

q: An enzyme moves two electrons from NADH to molecule X. Which statement is correct?
options: NADH is reduced and molecule X is oxidized
Both molecules are oxidized: electrons are moving between them
NADH is oxidized and molecule X is reduced
Neither molecule changes: moving electrons is not a chemical reaction

q: What drives the bulk flow of blood along a blood vessel?
options: The concentration gradient of oxygen along the vessel
The pressure difference between its two ends
The high pressure at the start of the vessel, whatever the pressure at its end
The viscosity of the blood

q: The pressure at the start of a tube is 100 mm Hg and at the end is 20 mm Hg. The tube's resistance is 4 mm Hg for each mL/min. What is the flow?
options: 25 mL/min
320 mL/min
20 mL/min
30 mL/min

q: The radius of a tube is cut to half its original value. The pressures at both ends stay the same, and so do the tube's length and the fluid. What happens to the flow?
options: It falls to 1/2 of the original
It falls to 1/4 of the original
It is unchanged: pressure alone sets the flow
It falls to 1/16 of the original
misconception: halving the radius halves the flow

q: Muscle in the wall of a small artery relaxes, and the artery's radius doubles. The pressure gradient across it does not change. By what factor does blood flow through it change?
options: It becomes 2 times larger
It becomes 16 times larger
It becomes 4 times larger
It becomes one-sixteenth as large

q: Two identical tubes carry the same fluid. Tube A has 150 mm Hg at its inlet and 140 mm Hg at its outlet. Tube B has 40 mm Hg at its inlet and 10 mm Hg at its outlet. Which statement is correct?
options: Tube A carries more flow: its pressures are much higher
Both carry the same flow: they are identical tubes
Tube B carries three times the flow of tube A
Neither carries flow: the outlets are not at 0 mm Hg
misconception: higher pressure means more flow

q: A nurse notices that an IV infusion is running slowly. The bag is hanging 50 cm above the patient's arm. She raises it to 100 cm above the arm and changes nothing else. Why does the fluid now run faster?
options: The taller fluid column raises the pressure at the catheter, widening ΔP
Raising the bag lowers the viscosity of the fluid in the tubing
Raising the bag stretches and widens the catheter
The fluid gains kinetic energy while the bag is lifted and keeps it

q: A paramedic needs to give fluid as fast as possible to a patient who is bleeding heavily. Starting from one IV setup, which single change would raise flow the most?
options: Doubling the pressure squeezing the fluid bag, using a pressure bag
Using a catheter of the same radius but half the length
Switching to a catheter with twice the internal radius and the same length
Warming the fluid enough to lower its viscosity by one-quarter

q: A clamp narrows a tube carrying fluid. The pressures at the inlet and outlet are held constant. Predict each change.

variables.name: Pressure gradient between inlet and outlet

q: Which changes would increase the resistance of a tube to the flow of a fluid? Select all that apply.
options: Making the tube longer
Raising the pressure at the inlet
Replacing the fluid with a more viscous one
Narrowing the tube's radius
Lowering the pressure at the outlet

q: Put the steps in order to show how tightening the muscle in a small artery's wall reduces blood flow through it, with the pressure gradient unchanged.
options: Muscle in the artery wall contracts
The artery's radius shrinks
The radius to the fourth power shrinks much more
Resistance rises steeply
Flow falls: the same pressure gradient is divided by a larger resistance

q: A tube has an inlet pressure of 90 mm Hg, an outlet pressure of 10 mm Hg and a flow of 20 mL/min. Fill the gap in this calculation of its resistance. ΔP = 90 − 10 = 80 mm Hg → R = ΔP ÷ F = ______ → R = 4 mm Hg for each mL/min.
A student works through what happens when a tube's radius is halved. One step is wrong. Find it.
options: At the start, ΔP = 80 mm Hg and R = 2 mm Hg for each mL/min, so F = 40 mL/min.
The radius is halved; the pressures, length and fluid stay the same.
The radius to the fourth power becomes (½)⁴ = 1/16 of its old value.
Resistance therefore doubles, from 2 to 4 mm Hg for each mL/min.
The new flow is found with F = ΔP / R, using the new resistance.

q: A patient's blood pressure is recorded as 120/80 mm Hg. What does the 120 mean?
options: 120 mm Hg above the surrounding air pressure, at the peak of each beat
120 mm Hg in total, counting the air pressure
A 120 mm column of blood pushed up by each beat
120 mm Hg below the surrounding air pressure, between beats

q: A 28-year-old man loses about 1.5 liters of blood from a deep leg wound. His blood pressure falls from 124/78 to 92/60 mm Hg. Which explanation fits?
options: Less blood in the same stretchy vessels stretches their walls less
His remaining blood has thickened and now lowers the pressure
The air pressure around him has fallen during the bleeding
His blood vessels have lengthened and now lower the pressure

q: Compared with lying flat, what happens to the pressure in the blood vessels of your feet when you stand up?
options: It falls: blood drains away from the feet when you stand
It rises by roughly 90 mm Hg from the weight of the blood column above them
It stays the same: the heart pumps at the same pressure either way
It rises by about 760 mm Hg: the atmospheric pressure is added

q: On a hot day the air is 40 °C and your skin is 34 °C. Which way does heat move between your skin and the air?
options: From your skin to the air
In neither direction
In both directions equally
From the air to your skin

q: A patient's blood has an unusually high concentration of cells. If the pressure gradient driving blood through a vessel stays the same, what happens to flow through that vessel?
options: It rises: more cells carry more blood through the vessel
It stays the same: the pressure gradient has not changed
It falls: thicker blood raises the resistance
It falls: the thick blood narrows the vessel

q: Which of these are examples of bulk flow? Select all that apply.
options: Blood moving along an artery
A drop of dye slowly spreading through a still glass of water
Air moving into your lungs as you breathe in
Fluid running from an IV bag into a vein
Heat spreading from your warm hand into a cold metal rail

q: An artery's radius shrinks by 10%, to 0.9 of its original value, while the pressure gradient stays the same. About how much flow remains?
options: About 90% of the original
About 66% of the original
About 50% of the original
About 10% of the original

q: Which of these is the steepest concentration gradient?
options: A difference of 20 mmol/L across 10 mm
A difference of 10 mmol/L across 1 mm
A difference of 50 mmol/L across 100 mm
A difference of 5 mmol/L across 5 mm

q: A drop of dye has spread evenly through a glass of still water. What are the dye particles doing now?
options: They have stopped moving because the gradient is gone
They are all drifting slowly toward the bottom of the glass
They keep moving at random, crossing any line each way in equal numbers
They move only when the water is stirred or warmed
misconception: particles stop moving at equilibrium

q: In your lungs, oxygen's pressure is higher in the air than in the blood arriving from your body, and carbon dioxide's pressure is lower. What happens across the thin barrier between them?
options: Oxygen diffuses into the blood while carbon dioxide diffuses out of it
Oxygen diffuses into the blood, and carbon dioxide stays in the blood until the oxygen has finished
Both gases diffuse into the blood, because blood moves faster than air
Neither gas crosses until the heart pushes it across

q: A container is divided by a membrane that lets water cross but not glucose. Both sides start as equal volumes of pure water. You dissolve glucose in side B. Predict each change over the next hour.

variables.name: Volume of fluid on side A
Volume of fluid on side B
Amount of glucose on side A
Osmolarity of side B, compared with just after the glucose was added

q: A substance takes 3 seconds to diffuse across a layer of tissue. The layer becomes three times as thick. Roughly how long does the same trip take now?
options: About 9 seconds
About 27 seconds
About 1 second
About 18 seconds

q: Which changes would speed the net diffusion of oxygen across a barrier? Select all that apply.
options: Doubling the surface area of the barrier
Making the barrier thicker
Raising the oxygen concentration on the high side
Replacing oxygen with a much larger particle
Making the barrier thinner

q: Mr. Patel, 70, has a weak heart, and fluid has collected in his lungs, thickening the barrier between the air and his blood. The oxygen in the air he breathes is normal, yet his blood oxygen is low. Which factor in diffusion has changed most?
options: The temperature of the air and blood
The size of the oxygen molecule
The concentration of oxygen in the air he is breathing in
The diffusion distance oxygen must cross between the air and his blood

q: A membrane that lets water cross, but not sodium chloride or glucose, separates two solutions. Side A holds 100 mmol/L sodium chloride. Side B holds 150 mmol/L glucose. Which way does water move?
options: From side A to side B, toward the higher number of millimoles
In neither direction, because the solutes are different substances
From side B to side A, toward the higher particle count
In neither direction, because neither solute can cross

q: A membrane that lets only water cross separates 150 mmol/L sodium chloride from 300 mmol/L glucose. What happens to the water?
options: Water moves into the glucose side, which has more millimoles per liter
Water moves into the sodium chloride side, because salt holds water more strongly
Water moves into the glucose side, because glucose molecules are larger
There is no net water movement: both sides have 300 mOsm/L

q: A marathon runner drinks far more plain water than she sweats out. Her blood becomes more dilute. What happens to her brain cells?
options: Water moves out of them, and they shrink
Water moves into them, and they swell
Salt diffuses out of them into her blood, and their size is unchanged
Nothing happens, because brain cells are protected by the skull

q: A membrane lets both water and substance X cross freely. Side A holds a solution of X; side B holds pure water. What is the state after a long time?
options: Side A ends up holding more water, because X keeps drawing water toward it
Side B holds all of X, because X moves away from where it is concentrated
X evens out on both sides, and neither side gains water for good
Nothing crosses at all, because both sides started out at the same pressure

q: What does a solution's osmotic pressure measure?
options: The pressure needed to stop water moving into it by osmosis
The pressure the solution exerts on the walls of its container
The pressure a pump must supply to push the solution along a tube
The pressure of the air above the solution

q: In panel B, three EPSPs from input E1 reach threshold, although one EPSP from the same input (panel A) does not. Why?

fig.alt: Four small graphs of membrane potential at a neuron trigger zone against time, 0 to 40 milliseconds, each with dashed lines at rest, minus 70, and threshold, minus 55. A, one EPSP: excitatory input E1 fires once, and the membrane rises about 6 millivolts, then fades back to rest without reaching threshold. B, temporal summation: E1 fires three times, 3 milliseconds apart; each small depolarization starts before the last has faded, so they stack up to threshold and an action potential fires. C, spatial summation: inputs E1, E2 and E3 fire at the same moment; their depolarizations add into one large one that reaches threshold, and an action potential fires. D, EPSP plus IPSP: E1 and inhibitory input I1 fire together; the depolarization and hyperpolarization nearly cancel, and the membrane barely moves from rest.

q: In panel D, an excitatory input and an inhibitory input fire together and the membrane barely moves. What would make this neuron reach threshold?

Across the arterioles, pressure falls steeply and the swings die away
In the capillaries, pressure rises again as blood slows down
In the veins, pressure falls slowly to near zero at the right atrium

q: A seated patient's blood pressure is measured with her arm hanging by her side, so the cuff is about 26 cm below her heart. At heart level her pressure is 124/78. Each centimeter of blood adds about 0.77 mm Hg. What will the cuff read?

5.2 L/min
1.2 L/min

q: A patient's cardiac output is 6.0 L/min and her heart rate is 75 beats/min. What is her stroke volume?

0.8 mL
80 mL

q: A patient starts taking a beta blocker, a drug that blocks beta-1 adrenergic receptor proteins in the heart. Predict the change in each variable at rest, compared with before the drug.
A person lying flat raises both legs, and blood pooled in the leg veins flows back toward the heart, increasing venous return. Before any reflex acts, predict the change in each variable.

Each action potential lasts longer

The peak of each action potential reaches a higher voltage

With sympathetic stimulation, it starts higher, near minus 50, and drifts up faster, so it fires more often.

q: In the parasympathetic stimulation trace, which two changes together slow the heart rate?

The threshold rises and the action potentials shrink
It stays depolarized longer and the threshold falls
It fires quickly but pauses at threshold between beats

With sympathetic stimulation, it starts higher, near minus 50, and drifts up faster, so it fires more often.

q: Why does stretching a ventricle during filling make its next contraction stronger?
options: It triggers a sympathetic reflex that releases norepinephrine onto the ventricle
It improves filament overlap and troponin's calcium sensitivity
It opens extra L-type calcium channels, letting more calcium in
It lengthens the action potential's plateau phase in every cell

q: For a few beats, a person's right ventricle ejects 5 mL more per beat than her left ventricle. Within a few beats, the two outputs match again, with no change in nerve signals. What restores the match?
options: The vagus nerve slowing the right ventricle
The pulmonary valve partly closing to limit right-sided output
The Frank–Starling mechanism in the left ventricle
Circulating epinephrine raising left ventricular contractility

q: Mr. Liu's aortic valve has narrowed and stiffened, so his left ventricle must generate a much higher pressure to eject blood. Which volume changes first, and which way?
options: End-diastolic volume falls
End-systolic volume falls
End-systolic volume rises
End-diastolic volume rises

q: What is afterload?
options: The stretch on ventricular muscle at the end of filling
The pressure a ventricle must overcome to open its valve and eject blood
The volume left in the ventricle after it contracts
The strength of contraction at a given stretch

q: Select every factor that increases contractility (a positive inotropic factor).
options: Norepinephrine on beta-1 receptor proteins
Hyperkalemia
Epinephrine from the adrenal medulla
A calcium channel blocker
Thyroid hormones
Acidosis

q: A patient's heart rate is 38 beats/min, and she feels faint. A paramedic gives atropine, a drug that blocks muscarinic receptor proteins. What happens to her heart rate?
options: It falls
It rises
It stays the same

q: Put the steps in order to show how sympathetic stimulation increases stroke volume.
options: Sympathetic nerves release norepinephrine onto ventricular muscle
Norepinephrine binds beta-1 adrenergic receptor proteins
Cyclic AMP rises inside the cardiac muscle cells
More calcium enters through L-type channels and more is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
More cross-bridges form and the contraction is stronger
End-systolic volume falls and stroke volume rises

q: An abnormal rhythm raises a patient's heart rate from 180 to 220 beats/min, and his cardiac output falls from 5.4 to 4.4 L/min. What best explains the fall?
options: The SA node is exhausted and fires weaker impulses
Filling time is too short for the ventricles to fill
Afterload rises sharply at fast heart rates
The ventricles contract too forcefully

q: A 70-year-old has a resting cardiac output of 4.5 L/min. His highest cardiac output on an exercise test is 13.5 L/min. What is his cardiac reserve?
options: 9.0 L/min

3.0 L/min
13.5 L/min

q: A student described how the parasympathetic system slows the heart. One step is wrong. Which one?
options: The cardioinhibitory center in the medulla oblongata increases its output
Signals travel down the vagus nerves to the heart
Vagal fibers release norepinephrine at the SA node
Extra potassium channels open and the funny current falls
The pacemaker potential takes longer to reach threshold

q: Complete the equation: cardiac output = heart rate × ____.
options: Stroke volume
End-diastolic volume
Ejection fraction
Mean arterial pressure

q: A drug raises contractility. Before the drug, EDV is 130 mL and ESV is 60 mL. After it, EDV is still 130 mL but ESV is 40 mL. By how much has stroke volume changed?
options: Up by 10 mL
Up by 20 mL
Down by 20 mL
Up by 40 mL

q: Where is the cardiovascular center that contains the cardioaccelerator and cardioinhibitory centers?
options: Hypothalamus
Cerebral cortex
Medulla oblongata
SA node

q: After a heart transplant, a patient's new heart has no nerve connections to his brain. When he starts walking briskly, his cardiac output still rises, though more slowly than before. Which pair of mechanisms can explain the rise?
options: The Frank–Starling mechanism and adrenal epinephrine
The vagus nerve and the cardioaccelerator center
Sympathetic nerves in the cardiac plexus and acetylcholine
The cardioinhibitory center and a longer filling time

q: Which Starling force pulls fluid from the interstitial fluid into a capillary?
options: Capillary hydrostatic pressure
Blood colloid osmotic pressure
Interstitial fluid colloid osmotic pressure
Arterial systolic pressure

q: At one point along a capillary, capillary hydrostatic pressure is 30 mm Hg, interstitial fluid hydrostatic pressure is 2 mm Hg, blood colloid osmotic pressure is 26 mm Hg and interstitial fluid colloid osmotic pressure is 4 mm Hg. options: −6 mm Hg, reabsorption into the capillary
+10 mm Hg, filtration out of the capillary
+6 mm Hg, filtration out of the capillary
+2 mm Hg, filtration out of the capillary

q: Near the venule end of a capillary, CHP is 18 mm Hg, IFHP is 1 mm Hg, BCOP is 25 mm Hg and IFCOP is 3 mm Hg. What net filtration pressure do the four forces give?
options: +7 mm Hg
−5 mm Hg
−9 mm Hg
+5 mm Hg

q: Mrs. Lindqvist, 61, has long-term liver disease. Her blood albumin is well below normal, and both of her ankles are swollen; pressing the skin leaves a dent. Which change best explains the swelling?
options: Her capillary hydrostatic pressure has risen
Her capillary walls have become leaky to protein
Her blood colloid osmotic pressure has fallen
Her interstitial fluid hydrostatic pressure has fallen
misconception: edema means there is too much blood in the tissue

q: Within minutes of twisting his ankle, a soccer player's ankle is swollen. His blood pressure and blood proteins are normal. Which explanation fits the rapid swelling best?
options: Histamine makes the capillaries leaky, so proteins escape into the tissue
The injury raises arterial pressure and so capillary pressure throughout his leg
Injured cells release albumin, raising the colloid osmotic pressure of the ankle's blood
Pain signals close the ankle's capillaries, trapping blood inside the injured tissue

q: Plasma contains far more sodium ions than protein molecules. Why do plasma proteins, and not sodium, create the osmotic pull that holds fluid in capillaries?
options: Endothelial cells actively pump sodium ions back out of the capillary
Charged particles such as sodium ions cannot cause osmosis
Osmotic pressure depends on solute mass, and proteins are far heavier
Sodium crosses the wall freely and evens out; proteins are held back

q: Which changes would increase net filtration out of the capillaries in a tissue? Select all that apply.
options: The arterioles feeding the tissue dilate
Pressure in the veins draining the tissue rises
Plasma albumin concentration falls
The arterioles feeding the tissue constrict
Plasma albumin concentration rises
The capillary walls become leaky to protein

q: A person's plasma protein concentration falls steadily over several weeks because of a very protein-poor diet. Predict the change in each variable once the protein level has fallen.
A cashier stands almost motionless at a register for six hours. Predict the change in each variable in the capillaries of her feet, compared with when she was lying down.

variables.name: Capillary hydrostatic pressure in the feet
Fluid in the tissues of her feet

q: A healthy adult rapidly loses about 800 mL of blood from a leg wound, and the bleeding is then stopped. Predict each variable, first right after the bleed and then over the following hours as the body compensates.

variables.name: Capillary hydrostatic pressure, right after the bleed
Net movement of interstitial fluid into the plasma, in the first hour
Plasma protein concentration, several hours later

q: Put the steps in sequence to show how kidney damage that lets protein leak into the urine leads to swelling of the legs.
options: Albumin is lost from the blood into the urine
Plasma albumin concentration falls
Blood colloid osmotic pressure falls
Net filtration pressure in systemic capillaries rises
Fluid filters out faster than it drains away
Interstitial fluid collects, first in the lowest parts of the body

q: This pathway explains swelling after a bee sting, but one step is wrong. Find the wrong step.
options: Histamine is released in the stung tissue
Gaps between the endothelial cells of nearby capillaries widen
Plasma proteins leak into the interstitial fluid
Interstitial fluid colloid osmotic pressure falls
Net filtration rises, and fluid collects in the tissue

q: In the revised Starling principle, sustained reabsorption shuts itself off. Complete the sequence: capillary hydrostatic pressure falls below the effective oncotic pull → fluid begins flowing into the capillary through the clefts → ____ → inward flow fades within minutes.
options: Interstitial proteins build up in the space beneath the glycocalyx
Plasma proteins leak out through the clefts into the interstitial fluid
The arterioles dilate and raise the capillary pressure back up
The glycocalyx dissolves, making the capillary wall fully permeable
misconception: capillaries reabsorb most filtered fluid at the venule end

q: According to the revised Starling principle, in most tissues at steady state, how does the fluid filtered out of capillaries get back into the blood?
options: It is reabsorbed at the venule end of the same capillaries it left
It diffuses into body cells and is released later as they die
It enters drainage vessels that return it to veins near the heart
It evaporates through the skin and is replaced by drinking water
misconception: capillaries reabsorb most filtered fluid at the venule end

q: In the classic textbook picture of capillary exchange that most exams expect, what happens at the venule end of a capillary, and which force is larger there?
options: Net filtration; capillary hydrostatic pressure is larger
Net reabsorption; blood colloid osmotic pressure is larger
No net movement; the two forces are equal
Net reabsorption; capillary hydrostatic pressure is larger

q: Raising venous pressure by 10 mm Hg increases filtration in a capillary bed much more than raising arterial pressure by 10 mm Hg. What explains the difference?
options: Veins have thicker walls than arteries, so they pass pressure changes on better
A rise in arterial pressure lowers blood colloid osmotic pressure and cancels out
Venous blood carries much more plasma protein than the arterial blood does
Arteriole resistance upstream of the capillaries absorbs most arterial changes

q: A small water-soluble drug given by vein reaches the interstitial fluid of skeletal muscle within minutes but barely enters the brain tissue. What difference between these capillaries best explains this?
options: Brain capillaries are sinusoids with wide gaps between cells
Brain capillaries have sealed clefts between their endothelial cells
Brain capillaries have a much higher hydrostatic pressure
Muscle capillaries lack an endothelial lining

q: During a sprint, oxygen delivery from blood to the leg muscle cells rises sharply. Apart from the steeper oxygen gradient, which change in the capillary bed speeds diffusion?
options: Higher capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes oxygen out faster by bulk flow
More capillaries open, adding surface area and shortening the distance
The capillary walls thicken and store extra oxygen
Plasma proteins carry the oxygen out through the clefts
misconception: diffusion and filtration are the same process

q: Which substances cross a continuous capillary wall mainly by dissolving through the endothelial cells' plasma membranes? Select all that apply.
options: Oxygen
Glucose
Carbon dioxide
Sodium ions
Albumin

q: The arterioles supplying the skin constrict strongly for about 30 minutes. What happens to fluid exchange in the skin's capillaries during that time?
options: Capillary pressure falls; filtration slows and may briefly reverse
Capillary pressure rises, so filtration speeds up and the skin swells
Blood colloid osmotic pressure falls, so filtration speeds up in the skin
Nothing changes: arteriole diameter has no effect on the capillaries downstream

q: Where are the main arterial baroreceptors that drive the baroreceptor reflex?
options: In the walls of the right atrium and the venae cavae
In the carotid sinuses and the aortic arch
In the medulla oblongata and the hypothalamus
In the walls of the arterioles of each organ

q: A patient has a cardiac output of 4.5 L/min and a total peripheral resistance of 20 mm Hg·min/L. A drug then lowers TPR by 20 percent, and cardiac output does not change. What is the new mean arterial pressure?
options: 70 mm Hg
86 mm Hg
72 mm Hg
112 mm Hg

q: A healthy 25-year-old stands up quickly after lying down for an hour. Predict the change in each variable during the first several seconds of standing, before the baroreceptor reflex has had time to act.

options: Mean arterial pressure falls
The carotid sinus and aortic arch walls stretch less, and baroreceptors fire less
Fewer impulses reach the medulla oblongata in the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves
The cardiovascular center raises sympathetic output and lowers vagal output
Heart rate, contractility and arteriole constriction increase
Mean arterial pressure rises back toward its set point

q: This pathway describes the baroreceptor reflex after a sudden rise in blood pressure, but one step is wrong. Find the wrong step.

Baroreceptors fire more action potentials
The cardiovascular center receives more afferent impulses

Sympathetic output to the arterioles falls
Heart rate and TPR fall, and pressure comes back down

q: Complete the sequence: blood pressure falls → baroreceptors fire fewer action potentials → fewer impulses reach the medulla oblongata → ____ → heart rate and TPR rise.

The baroreceptors release norepinephrine directly onto the SA node
The arterioles relax, and more blood flows back into the veins

His arterioles cannot constrict in response to norepinephrine

q: A person's mean arterial pressure rises to a new, higher level and stays there for a week. Why does the baroreceptor reflex not bring it back down?

Renin converts angiotensinogen into angiotensin I

q: Which change would reduce renin release from the kidneys?

q: A student drinks 1.5 L of plain water in twenty minutes. An hour later she passes a large volume of very dilute urine. Which change explains this?

q: In right-sided heart failure, what causes the swelling in the ankles?

q: A plaque narrows a short segment of artery from a radius of 3 mm to a radius of 2 mm. By roughly how much does that segment's resistance rise?

q: At high altitude, a climber's ventilation keeps rising over the first week even though the air's PO2 has not changed. What mainly explains the continued rise?
options: Rising hematocrit makes the blood thicker and harder to oxygenate
The kidneys excrete bicarbonate and the central brake eases
The lungs grow new alveoli
The cortex learns to breathe voluntarily

q: In moderate steady exercise, ventilation may triple while arterial PCO2 and PO2 barely change. What does this tell you about the drive to breathe during exercise?
options: It comes from the carotid bodies sensing a fall in arterial PO2
Carbon dioxide production must not rise during exercise
Most of the drive does not come from blood-gas changes
The Hering–Breuer reflex is the main drive

q: Someone walks into a smoky room and starts coughing, with a tight feeling in the chest. Which sensory receptors triggered this?
options: Lung stretch receptors in airway smooth muscle
Central chemoreceptors in the medulla oblongata
Irritant receptors in the airway lining
Aortic bodies

q: Which spirometry result confirms the airflow obstruction of COPD?
options: FEV1 ÷ FVC below 0.70 after an airway-opening drug
FEV1 ÷ FVC above 0.90 on a test done before any drug
A total lung capacity well below the predicted normal value
A vital capacity that doubles after albuterol

q: After albuterol, a patient's FVC is 4.0 L and her FEV1 is 2.4 L. What is her FEV1 ÷ FVC, and what does it show?
options: 1.67: restrictive disease
0.60: airflow obstruction
0.60: normal for her age and size
0.85: airflow obstruction

q: Emphysema destroys many alveolar walls in a man's lungs. Predict the change in each variable, compared with healthy lungs.
Using the lung volumes in the figure, which band becomes larger in severe emphysema?
options: Tidal volume
Inspiratory reserve volume
Vital capacity
Residual volume

fig.alt: Two panels on a vertical scale from 0 to 6,000 milliliters. The left panel is a spirogram: a trace of lung volume over time shows small, regular breaths between about 2,500 and 2,900 mL, one deepest possible breath in to 6,000 mL, and one fullest possible breath out to about 1,200 mL. Colored bands behind the trace mark the four volumes: residual volume from 0 to about 1,200 mL, expiratory reserve volume up to about 2,500 mL, tidal volume up to about 2,900 mL, and inspiratory reserve volume up to 6,000 mL. The right panel shows the capacities as bars built from those volumes: inspiratory capacity above functional residual capacity; vital capacity above residual volume; and total lung capacity spanning the whole scale.

q: Why do the smallest airways collapse during expiration in emphysema but not in healthy lungs?
options: Their smooth muscle goes into spasm with each breath out
Mucus plugs block them
They have lost the elastic fibers that held them open
Their cartilage rings have been dissolved

q: How is chronic bronchitis defined?
options: Destruction of alveolar walls seen on a CT scan of the chest
Episodes of wheezing that fully reverse with albuterol
An infection of the alveoli with fever
A daily cough with mucus for 3 months in each of 2 years

q: Select every feature that is typical of emphysema rather than chronic bronchitis or asthma.
options: Destruction of alveolar walls
Raised lung compliance
Daily cough with large amounts of mucus
Reduced diffusion of gases across the lung
Obstruction that reverses fully with albuterol
Enlarged mucus glands in the airway walls

q: Two patients each have FEV1 ÷ FVC of 0.55. After inhaling albuterol, Ms. Rao's ratio rises to 0.80; Mr. Dunn's rises only to 0.58. Which pairing is most likely?
options: Ms. Rao has emphysema; Mr. Dunn has asthma
Both have pulmonary edema
Ms. Rao has asthma; Mr. Dunn has COPD
Both have restrictive disease
misconception: asthma and COPD are the same disease

q: A paramedic finds Mr. Chen, who has severe COPD, breathless with an SpO2 of 80%. What is the best-supported approach to oxygen?
options: Withhold oxygen, because it will remove his hypoxic drive and stop his breathing
Give only room air until his PCO2 is measured
Give maximal oxygen and aim for 100% saturation
Give oxygen to a target of about 88–92% and watch his breathing
misconception: oxygen should be withheld in COPD because of the hypoxic drive

q: After years of severe COPD, a patient develops swollen ankles and an enlarged right ventricle. What links the lung disease to the heart?
options: Chronic hypoxic vasoconstriction raises right ventricular afterload
Low oxygen weakens the left ventricle, which backs blood into the lungs
Mucus from the lungs blocks the coronary arteries
Polycythemia makes the right ventricle fill with too little blood

q: A man with long-standing COPD and low blood oxygen has a hematocrit of 56%. What caused the high hematocrit?
options: Dehydration from rapid breathing
Carbon dioxide retention stimulating the bone marrow directly to divide
Chronic hypoxemia stimulating erythropoietin release from the kidneys
Smoke damaging the spleen

q: Mrs. Ito has severe left-sided heart failure and wakes up gasping, with crackles in both lungs. What mainly drives fluid into her lungs?
options: A leak in the respiratory membrane caused by infection
Low blood colloid osmotic pressure from liver failure
Blocked lymphatic vessels in the lungs
Raised hydrostatic pressure in her pulmonary capillaries

q: In early pulmonary edema, a patient's arterial PO2 is low but his PCO2 is normal or slightly low. Why is oxygen affected first?
options: Edema fluid reacts with oxygen
Carbon dioxide is far more soluble and diffuses more readily
Carbon dioxide leaves the blood by a route that avoids the membrane
Hemoglobin releases carbon dioxide faster when fluid is present

q: Why does a patient with left-sided heart failure become more breathless when lying flat?
options: More venous return raises pressure in the pulmonary capillaries
The weight of the chest compresses both lungs when lying down
Lying flat stops the diaphragm from contracting fully
Lying flat lowers the colloid osmotic pressure of the blood plasma

q: A patient with sepsis develops pulmonary edema, although his heart pumps normally and his pulmonary capillary pressure is normal. What is the mechanism?
options: Raised capillary hydrostatic pressure caused by a failing left ventricle
Inflammation makes the respiratory membrane leak fluid and proteins
Too little surfactant is made because of fever
Air leaks into the pleural cavity

q: Mr. Osei has pneumonia filling his right lower lobe. On high-flow oxygen, his SpO2 rises only from 86% to 90%. Why does oxygen help so little?
options: Blood past the filled alveoli never meets the extra oxygen
Bacteria in the lung consume the extra oxygen
High-flow oxygen blocks the respiratory centers
His hemoglobin has lost its ability to bind oxygen

q: Put the steps in order to show how tuberculosis infection develops and can later become active.
options: A person breathes in tiny airborne droplets carrying the bacteria
Alveolar macrophages engulf the bacteria
The bacteria survive and multiply inside the macrophages
T cells activate the macrophages and a granuloma walls off the infection
The bacteria stay dormant for years as latent infection
Immunity weakens and the bacteria break out as active disease

q: A student described how smoking causes emphysema. One step is wrong. Which one?
options: Smoke draws neutrophils and macrophages into the lungs
These cells release protein-digesting enzymes
Smoke inactivates alpha-1 antitrypsin, which normally blocks the enzymes
Elastic fibers in alveolar walls are broken down
The lungs become stiffer and less compliant
Small airways collapse during expiration and trap air

q: Fill the gap: left ventricle fails → pressure rises in the left atrium and pulmonary veins → ____ → fluid collects around and in the alveoli.
options: Pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure rises
The blood colloid osmotic pressure in the lungs rises
Lymph flow from the lungs stops
The respiratory membrane becomes leaky

q: A woman's TB skin test is positive. She has no symptoms and a normal chest X-ray. What is her status?
options: Latent TB infection that is not contagious
Active tuberculosis that spreads by coughing
No infection: a positive test without symptoms is a false result
Pneumonia caused by the TB vaccine

q: A man with emphysema breathes out slowly through pursed lips. How does this help him?
options: It warms the air before it reaches the alveoli
It strengthens his diaphragm
It raises the oxygen content of the air he breathes in
It holds collapsing small airways open longer

q: Which disorder mainly causes air to reach alveoli that receive no blood, rather than blood reaching alveoli that receive no air?
options: Pneumonia
Pulmonary edema at the alveolar stage
Pulmonary embolism
Asthma
